- ✗ **C. Weighted routing without checks:** without health checks, Route 53 keeps returning the failed Region's record in proportion to its weight, so part of the traffic still goes to the outage.
- ✗ **D. Hard-coded static IP:** clients always connect to one address; moving traffic to another Region would need an app update, and DNS-based failover cannot help at all.

## Key idea
DNS-level Regional failover means Route 53 failover records with a health check on the primary; routing policies without health checks keep sending users to a dead endpoint.

stem: Private instances in three AZs use a single NAT gateway. Which change improves availability?

choices.text: Move all instances into the AZ that hosts the NAT gateway
Create a NAT gateway in each AZ and route each AZ to its own
Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance of a larger size
Add a second internet gateway to the VPC for redundancy

explanation:
## NAT gateways are zonal
A NAT gateway lets instances in private subnets reach the internet (for updates or APIs) while blocking inbound connections. Each NAT gateway is created in one subnet, so it lives in one AZ. It is redundant within that AZ, but it goes down if that AZ fails.
## The problem with one shared NAT gateway
If private subnets in `az-a`, `az-b` and `az-c` all route `0.0.0.0/0` to one NAT gateway in `az-a`:
- An outage in `az-a` cuts outbound internet access for all three AZs.
- Traffic from `az-b` and `az-c` also crosses AZs, adding data transfer charges.
## The fix
Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet of each AZ, and give each AZ's private subnets their own route table whose default route points to the NAT gateway in the same AZ.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Move everything into the NAT's AZ:** this removes the multi-AZ design entirely, so a single AZ failure now takes down the whole application.
- ✓ **B. One NAT gateway per AZ with per-AZ routes (correct):** the failure of one AZ only affects the instances in that AZ, and the other AZs keep outbound access.
- ✗ **C. Larger NAT instance:** a NAT instance is a single EC2 instance in one AZ that you must patch and fail over yourself; a bigger size adds bandwidth, not AZ redundancy.
- ✗ **D. Second internet gateway:** a VPC can have only one internet gateway attached, and the internet gateway is already a highly available, Region-wide component; the single point of failure is the NAT gateway.

## Key idea
NAT gateways are zonal, so high availability means one NAT gateway per AZ with each AZ routing to its own, not a bigger NAT or more internet gateways.

stem: An application needs shared file storage for Linux instances across multiple AZs that remains available if one AZ fails. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon EBS snapshots
Amazon EBS volume on one instance
Amazon EFS Regional file system
EC2 instance store volumes

explanation:
## Block storage versus shared file storage
- **Amazon EBS** is block storage that lives in one AZ. A standard volume attaches to one instance (Multi-Attach for `io1`/`io2` is limited to instances in the same AZ and needs a cluster-aware file system).
- **Instance store** is disk physically attached to the host; its data is lost when the instance stops or the host fails.
- **Amazon EFS** is a managed NFS file system. Many Linux instances can mount it at the same time.
## Regional EFS
An EFS file system of the **Regional** type (as opposed to One Zone) stores data redundantly across multiple AZs. You create a mount target in each AZ, and instances mount it through the NFS protocol, for example with `mount -t efs fs-12345678:/ /data`. If one AZ fails, instances in the other AZs keep reading and writing the same data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. EBS snapshots:** snapshots are point-in-time backups stored in S3; they cannot be mounted as a live shared file system, only restored into a new volume.
- ✗ **B. EBS volume on one instance:** the volume is tied to one AZ and one instance, so other instances cannot share it and an AZ failure makes it unavailable.
- ✓ **C. EFS Regional file system (correct):** it is shared, concurrent NFS storage for Linux with data stored across multiple AZs and mount targets in each AZ, so it stays available when one AZ fails.
- ✗ **D. Instance store:** it is local to one host, cannot be shared between instances, and its data is lost if the instance stops or the host fails.

## Key idea
Shared Linux file storage across AZs is EFS (Regional); EBS and instance store are single-AZ block storage for one instance.

stem: A company needs to recover a deleted DynamoDB item that was removed by mistake two days ago. Which feature allows this?

choices.text: Point-in-time recovery on the table
Time to live on table items
DynamoDB Streams on the table
DynamoDB Accelerator in front

explanation:
## Point-in-time recovery in DynamoDB
**Point-in-time recovery (PITR)** continuously backs up a DynamoDB table. Once enabled, you can restore the table to any second within the recovery period, which is up to the last 35 days (the period is configurable from 1 to 35 days).
## How a restore works
A PITR restore always creates a **new table**; it does not modify the existing one. To recover one deleted item:
- Restore the table to a time just before the deletion, for example 10:14 two days ago, into a new table.
- Read the item from the restored table and write it back into the production table.
- Delete the temporary table.
PITR must already be enabled before the mistake happens.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Point-in-time recovery (correct):** continuous backups let you restore the table to the moment before the item was deleted, then copy the item back.
- ✗ **B. Time to live:** TTL automatically deletes items after a timestamp attribute expires. It removes data; it has no way to bring a deleted item back.
- ✗ **C. DynamoDB Streams:** a stream keeps item-level change records for only 24 hours, so a deletion from two days ago is no longer available there, and a stream is not a restore feature.
- ✗ **D. DynamoDB Accelerator:** DAX is an in-memory read cache that speeds up reads; it holds no backups and cannot restore deleted data.

## Key idea
Recovering data deleted days ago needs a backup feature (PITR, up to 35 days); TTL deletes items, Streams keep only 24 hours and DAX is just a cache.

stem: A company needs an RPO of seconds and an RTO of minutes for its EC2-based application in a second Region at low ongoing cost. Which service fits?

choices.text: AMIs copied once a month
S3 Cross-Region Replication
Daily AWS Backup plans only
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery

explanation:
## RPO and RTO
- **RPO (recovery point objective)**: how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. An RPO of seconds means replication must be nearly continuous.
- **RTO (recovery time objective)**: how long recovery may take. An RTO of minutes means servers must be launchable quickly and automatically.
## How AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery works
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS) installs a replication agent on source servers and continuously replicates their disks at block level into a staging area in the target Region, using low-cost instances and storage. No full copy of the application runs until you need it.
- During a disaster or a drill, DRS launches recovery instances from the latest (or an earlier) point in time within minutes.
- Ongoing cost stays low because only the lightweight staging resources run day to day.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Monthly AMI copies:** an AMI copied once a month means up to a month of lost data, far from an RPO of seconds.
- ✗ **B. S3 Cross-Region Replication:** CRR copies objects in S3 buckets; it does not replicate EC2 instances or their EBS volumes, so it cannot recover the servers.
- ✗ **C. Daily AWS Backup plans:** a daily backup gives an RPO of up to 24 hours, and restoring and rebuilding instances takes longer than a few minutes.
- ✓ **D. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (correct):** continuous block-level replication gives an RPO of seconds, automated launch gives an RTO of minutes, and the low-cost staging area keeps ongoing cost down.

## Key idea
RPO of seconds needs continuous replication; for EC2 servers at low cost that is Elastic Disaster Recovery, not periodic backups or AMI copies.

stem: Which TWO services help build loosely coupled architectures? (Select TWO)

choices.text: AWS Direct Connect
Amazon EBS
Amazon EC2 Instance Store
Amazon EventBridge
Amazon SQS

explanation:
## What loose coupling means
In a **tightly coupled** system, component A calls component B directly and waits for it. If B is slow or down, A fails too. In a **loosely coupled** system, components communicate through an intermediary, so each one can fail, scale or change independently.
## Two AWS building blocks
- **Amazon SQS** is a message queue. A producer writes messages to the queue; consumers pull them when they are ready. If consumers are down, messages wait in the queue (retained for 4 days by default, up to 14 days).
- **Amazon EventBridge** is an event bus. Producers publish events such as `OrderPlaced`; rules match events and route them to targets such as Lambda, SQS or Step Functions. The producer does not need to know which consumers exist.
Example: the order service publishes `OrderPlaced` to EventBridge; one rule sends it to an SQS queue for billing, another to a Lambda function for email.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AWS Direct Connect:** it is a dedicated network connection between on-premises and AWS; it moves packets but provides no messaging or buffering between application components.
- ✗ **B. Amazon EBS:** it is block storage attached to an EC2 instance in one AZ; it stores data for that instance and does not pass messages between components.
- ✗ **C. Instance store:** it is temporary disk on the EC2 host, lost when the instance stops; it has nothing to do with communication between services.
- ✓ **D. Amazon EventBridge (correct):** an event bus decouples producers from consumers; producers publish events and rules route them to any number of targets without direct calls.
- ✓ **E. Amazon SQS (correct):** a queue buffers messages between producers and consumers, so each side can scale or fail independently and work is not lost when consumers are busy.

## Key idea
Loose coupling comes from messaging and eventing intermediaries such as SQS and EventBridge, not from storage or network links.

stem: Which TWO actions improve the availability of an application backed by Amazon Aurora? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Disable automated backups to reduce write overhead
Use the cluster endpoint so failover is transparent
Connect directly to the writer instance's IP address
Place all replicas in the writer's Availability Zone
Add Aurora Replicas in other Availability Zones

explanation:
## Aurora cluster layout
An Amazon Aurora cluster has one **writer** instance and up to 15 **Aurora Replicas** (readers). All instances share one cluster volume that stores six copies of the data across three AZs.
## Failover and endpoints
- If the writer fails, Aurora promotes one of the replicas to be the new writer, typically in well under a minute (often around 30 seconds). Without any replica, Aurora must re-create the writer, which takes much longer.
- The **cluster endpoint** is a DNS name that always points to the current writer. After failover, Aurora updates it to the new writer, so applications only need to reconnect with the same name.
- Instance IP addresses and instance endpoints refer to one specific instance, which may be the failed one.
Example: writer in `us-east-1a`, replicas in `1b` and `1c`. If `1a` fails, a replica in `1b` is promoted and the cluster endpoint now resolves to it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Disable automated backups:** Aurora automated backups cannot be turned off (retention is at least one day), and removing backups would only reduce recoverability; it adds no availability.
- ✓ **B. Cluster endpoint (correct):** it always resolves to the current writer, so after a failover the application reconnects to the new writer without any configuration change.
- ✗ **C. Writer's IP address:** the IP belongs to one instance; after a failover the writer is a different instance, so the application would keep connecting to the failed one.
- ✗ **D. All replicas in the writer's AZ:** if that AZ fails, the writer and every replica fail together, leaving no healthy instance to promote.
- ✓ **E. Replicas in other AZs (correct):** they are failover targets; if the writer or its whole AZ fails, a replica in a healthy AZ is promoted quickly.

## Key idea
Aurora availability comes from replicas in other AZs as failover targets plus connecting through the cluster endpoint, which follows the writer after failover.

stem: A company wants to process uploaded images asynchronously and automatically when they arrive in S3, without managing servers. Which design fits?

choices.text: A cron job on-premises that downloads new files
A Kinesis stream that users write images into
S3 event notifications invoking a Lambda function
An EC2 instance polling the bucket every minute

explanation:
## Event-driven processing with S3 and Lambda
Amazon S3 can publish **event notifications** when something happens in a bucket, for example `s3:ObjectCreated:*` when an object is uploaded. A notification can invoke an AWS Lambda function directly (or go through SQS, SNS or EventBridge).
## How it works
- A user uploads `photos/cat.jpg`.
- S3 invokes the Lambda function **asynchronously** with an event that contains the bucket name and object key.
- The function reads the image, creates a thumbnail and writes it to another prefix or bucket.
Lambda runs one execution per event and scales out automatically with the number of uploads; you pay only for the time the function runs, and there are no servers to patch.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. On-premises cron job:** it needs on-premises servers, runs only on a schedule instead of on arrival, and has to list and download objects over the internet.
- ✗ **B. Kinesis stream for images:** users would have to send images into the stream instead of S3, records have a small maximum size that large images can exceed, and consumers still need to be built and run.
- ✓ **C. S3 event notifications invoking Lambda (correct):** every upload triggers processing automatically and asynchronously, scaling with demand and with no servers to manage.
- ✗ **D. EC2 polling the bucket:** it requires a server that you manage, adds up to a minute of delay, and repeatedly lists the bucket even when nothing is new.

## Key idea
"Automatically when objects arrive, without servers" points to S3 event notifications triggering Lambda, not polling or scheduled jobs.

stem: A company must back up EC2, EBS, RDS, and EFS on a schedule with centralized retention policies. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Backup
AWS Storage Gateway
AWS DataSync
AWS Snowball

explanation:
## Centralized backup with AWS Backup
**AWS Backup** is a managed service that backs up many AWS resource types from one place, including EC2 instances, EBS volumes, RDS and Aurora databases, EFS file systems, DynamoDB tables and more.
## Key concepts
- **Backup plan**: a schedule (for example daily at 03:00) plus lifecycle rules such as "move to cold storage after 30 days, delete after 365 days".
- **Resource assignment**: select resources by tag (for example `backup=daily`) or by ARN, so new tagged resources are included automatically.
- **Backup vault**: where recovery points are stored, with its own encryption key and access policy; Vault Lock can prevent deletion before retention ends.
- With AWS Organizations, backup policies can be applied across many accounts.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. AWS Backup (correct):** it provides scheduled, policy-based backups with central retention rules for EC2, EBS, RDS, EFS and other services from one console.
- ✗ **B. AWS Storage Gateway:** it connects on-premises applications to AWS storage through file, volume and tape interfaces; it does not schedule backups of AWS resources such as RDS or EFS.
- ✗ **C. AWS DataSync:** it copies and synchronizes data between storage systems (for example NFS to EFS or S3), but it has no backup plans, recovery points or retention policies for EC2 or RDS.
- ✗ **D. AWS Snowball:** it is a physical device for moving large amounts of data offline into or out of AWS, not a scheduled backup service.

## Key idea
Scheduled backups with central retention across many AWS services is AWS Backup; Storage Gateway, DataSync and Snowball move data but do not manage backup policies.

stem: A company runs containers and wants AWS to manage the underlying servers so it only defines tasks and services. Which option fits?

choices.text: Kubernetes on on-premises VMs
Docker on a single EC2 host
Amazon ECS on self-managed EC2
Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate

explanation:
## Who manages the servers under containers?
Amazon ECS schedules containers as **tasks** (one or more containers defined in a task definition) and keeps a set number of tasks running as a **service**. ECS can run tasks on two kinds of capacity:
- **EC2 launch type**: you run and manage the EC2 container instances yourself: choosing instance types, patching the OS, scaling the cluster.
- **AWS Fargate**: AWS provides the compute for each task. You specify CPU and memory in the task definition (for example `0.5 vCPU`, `1 GB`) and never see or manage the underlying servers.
Fargate also works with Amazon EKS for Kubernetes pods.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Kubernetes on on-premises VMs:** the company must operate the VMs, the hypervisor and the Kubernetes control plane itself, which is the opposite of AWS-managed servers.
- ✗ **B. Docker on a single EC2 host:** the company manages the instance and the Docker setup, and a single host is also a single point of failure.
- ✗ **C. ECS on self-managed EC2:** ECS orchestrates the containers, but the company still manages the EC2 instances, including patching and capacity.
- ✓ **D. Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate (correct):** you define only tasks and services; AWS provisions, patches and scales the servers that run them.

## Key idea
For containers without managing servers choose Fargate; ECS on EC2 still leaves the instances to you.

stem: A company compares pilot light and warm standby DR strategies. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Pilot light runs full production capacity in both Regions at all times
Warm standby keeps only backups with no running resources in the second Region
Warm standby runs a scaled-down working copy, recovering faster than pilot light at higher cost
Pilot light always recovers faster than warm standby at a higher cost

explanation:
## The four AWS DR strategies
From cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest:
- **Backup and restore**: only backups in the recovery Region; everything is rebuilt after a disaster (RTO of hours).
- **Pilot light**: core data is replicated live (for example a database replica), but application servers are off or not yet created. Recovery means starting and scaling them (RTO of tens of minutes).
- **Warm standby**: a complete, working copy of the environment runs at reduced size. Recovery means scaling it up to full capacity (RTO of minutes).
- **Multi-site active/active**: full capacity in both Regions serving traffic (RTO near zero, highest cost).
## Pilot light versus warm standby
The difference is whether the application tier is already running. Warm standby can take some traffic immediately and only needs scaling, so it recovers faster, but it costs more because servers run all the time.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Pilot light runs full capacity:** full production capacity in both Regions describes multi-site active/active; pilot light keeps only core components such as data running.
- ✗ **B. Warm standby keeps only backups:** backups with no running resources is the backup and restore strategy; warm standby always has running resources.
- ✓ **C. Warm standby runs a scaled-down working copy (correct):** the whole stack is already running at small size, so recovery is only scale-up, making it faster than pilot light and more expensive.
- ✗ **D. Pilot light faster and more expensive:** it is the reverse; pilot light is cheaper because less runs, and slower because servers must be started and scaled.

## Key idea
Pilot light keeps only the core (data) running and is cheaper but slower; warm standby keeps a small full copy running and is faster but costs more.

stem: An application needs block storage with consistent high IOPS for a transactional database on EC2. Which EBS volume type fits best?

choices.text: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2)
Magnetic previous-generation disks
Cold HDD storage volumes (sc1)
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)

explanation:
## EBS volume families
- **SSD volumes** are built for IOPS (many small random reads and writes): `gp3` (general purpose) and `io2` (Provisioned IOPS).
- **HDD volumes** are built for throughput on large sequential reads: `st1` (Throughput Optimized) and `sc1` (Cold).
- **Magnetic (standard)** is a previous-generation type kept for older workloads.
## Provisioned IOPS SSD
With `io2` (all io2 volumes now run on EBS Block Express) you set the exact IOPS you need, up to 256,000 IOPS per volume, with sub-millisecond latency and consistent performance, plus higher durability (99.999%) than other EBS types. That consistency is what transactional databases such as busy Oracle, SQL Server or PostgreSQL workloads need.
Example: an OLTP database needs a steady 40,000 IOPS; provision an `io2` volume with 40,000 IOPS.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) (correct):** it delivers a guaranteed, consistent high IOPS level with low latency, exactly what a demanding transactional database requires.
- ✗ **B. Magnetic previous generation:** these volumes offer only around 100 IOPS on average with variable performance, far too little for a busy transactional database.
- ✗ **C. Cold HDD (sc1):** it is the lowest-cost type for rarely accessed, sequential data; its performance is measured in throughput, not IOPS, and random small I/O performs poorly.
- ✗ **D. Throughput Optimized HDD (st1):** it is designed for large sequential reads such as logs and big data; database random I/O needs SSD IOPS, and st1 cannot be a boot volume.

## Key idea
Consistent high IOPS for databases means SSD, specifically io2 Provisioned IOPS; HDD types (st1, sc1) are for sequential throughput.

stem: A big data job reads large files sequentially from block storage at high throughput, and cost matters. Which EBS type fits?

choices.text: Cold HDD storage (sc1)
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
General Purpose SSD (gp3)
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2)

explanation:
## Throughput versus IOPS
- **IOPS** counts input/output operations per second and matters for many small random reads and writes, such as databases.
- **Throughput** measures megabytes per second and matters for large sequential reads, such as scanning log files or big data sets.
## The EBS HDD types
- **Throughput Optimized HDD (`st1`)**: low-cost HDD for **frequently accessed**, throughput-heavy sequential workloads such as big data, data warehouses and log processing; up to 500 MiB/s per volume.
- **Cold HDD (`sc1`)**: the lowest cost per GB, for **infrequently accessed** data; up to 250 MiB/s per volume with lower baseline throughput.
SSD types (`gp3`, `io2`) can also be fast, but you pay SSD prices per GB for performance a sequential job does not need.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cold HDD (sc1):** it is meant for rarely accessed data; its lower baseline throughput makes a job that reads heavily and regularly slower than on st1.
- ✓ **B. Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) (correct):** it is built for frequently accessed, large sequential reads at high throughput and costs much less per GB than SSD.
- ✗ **C. General Purpose SSD (gp3):** it works but costs more per GB than st1, and its strength is balanced IOPS rather than cheap sequential throughput for large data sets.
- ✗ **D. Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2):** it is the most expensive type and pays for random IOPS that a sequential big data job does not use.

## Key idea
Large, frequent sequential reads at low cost means st1; sc1 is for cold data and SSD types pay for IOPS you do not need.

stem: Users worldwide upload large files to a single S3 bucket and experience slow uploads. Which feature helps?

choices.text: S3 Requester Pays mode
S3 Transfer Acceleration
S3 Object Lock settings
S3 Intelligent-Tiering

explanation:
## Why uploads from far away are slow
When a user in Sydney uploads to a bucket in `us-east-1`, the data travels over the public internet across many networks. Long distance and congested routes raise latency and packet loss, and TCP slows down.
## How S3 Transfer Acceleration works
Transfer Acceleration uses the CloudFront edge network. The client sends data to the nearest edge location, and from there it travels to the bucket over the AWS global network, which is faster and more reliable than the public internet over long distances.
- Enable it on the bucket, then use the accelerate endpoint, for example `mybucket.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com`.
- You pay an extra per-GB fee, charged only when acceleration actually improves the transfer.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Requester Pays:** it changes who pays for requests and downloads; it has no effect on network path or upload speed.
- ✓ **B. S3 Transfer Acceleration (correct):** uploads enter the AWS network at the nearest edge location and travel over the AWS backbone, speeding up long-distance transfers to a single bucket.
- ✗ **C. Object Lock:** it stores objects in write-once-read-many mode to prevent deletion or overwrite; it is a compliance feature, not a performance one.
- ✗ **D. Intelligent-Tiering:** it automatically moves objects between access tiers to lower storage cost based on access patterns; it does not change upload speed.

## Key idea
Slow long-distance uploads to one bucket are fixed with Transfer Acceleration (edge entry plus AWS backbone); storage classes and billing options do not affect speed.

stem: Large files uploaded to S3 often fail midway over unreliable networks. Which approach improves reliability and speed?

choices.text: Uploading files one byte at a time in sequence
Compressing files into one larger archive object
Multipart upload with parallel parts and retries
Single PUT requests with longer client timeouts

explanation:
## What multipart upload does
Multipart upload splits one object into parts that are uploaded separately and then combined by S3:
- `CreateMultipartUpload` starts the upload and returns an upload ID.
- `UploadPart` sends each part (5 MiB to 5 GiB, up to 10,000 parts); parts can be sent in parallel.
- `CompleteMultipartUpload` tells S3 to assemble the parts into one object.
## Why it helps on unreliable networks
- If one part fails, only that part is retried instead of the whole file.
- Parallel parts use more bandwidth, so large files finish faster.
- A single PUT is limited to 5 GB; larger objects, up to terabytes in size, must be uploaded with multipart upload.
Example: a 10 GB file in 100 MB parts; if part 57 fails, only those 100 MB are resent. AWS recommends multipart for objects larger than 100 MB, and the AWS CLI and SDKs use it automatically.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One byte at a time:** sending bytes sequentially would be extremely slow and still gives no resume or retry model; S3 has no API for byte-by-byte uploads.
- ✗ **B. One larger archive:** combining files makes the single object even bigger, so any network failure forces an even larger retransmission.
- ✓ **C. Multipart upload with parallel parts and retries (correct):** failures cost only one part instead of the whole file, and parallel parts increase speed.
- ✗ **D. Single PUT with longer timeouts:** a longer timeout does not help when the connection drops; the whole object must be resent after any failure, and a single PUT is capped at 5 GB.

## Key idea
For large uploads over unreliable links, multipart upload retries only failed parts and uploads in parallel; bigger objects or longer timeouts do not fix failures.

stem: A workload needs high compute performance for video encoding with many CPU cores. Which EC2 instance family fits?

choices.text: Compute optimized instances such as C family
Memory optimized instances such as R family
Burstable instances such as the T family
Storage optimized instances such as I family

explanation:
## EC2 instance families
EC2 instance types are grouped by the resource they emphasize:
- **Compute optimized (C family, for example `c7i`, `c7g`)**: high-performance processors and a high CPU-to-memory ratio.
- **Memory optimized (R, X families)**: much more RAM per vCPU.
- **Storage optimized (I, D families)**: fast local NVMe or large local disks.
- **Burstable (T family)**: low baseline CPU with credits to burst for short periods.
## Why video encoding fits compute optimized
Video encoding keeps every CPU core busy for long periods doing arithmetic on frames, while memory needs are moderate. C family instances deliver the most CPU performance per dollar for this kind of work; the same applies to batch processing, scientific modeling and game servers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Compute optimized C family (correct):** it offers high-performance CPUs with many cores at the best price per unit of compute, matching sustained CPU-heavy encoding.
- ✗ **B. Memory optimized R family:** it adds large amounts of RAM per vCPU, which encoding does not need, so you pay for memory that sits unused.
- ✗ **C. Burstable T family:** it runs at a low baseline CPU level and depends on credits; sustained encoding exhausts the credits and either throttles or incurs extra charges in unlimited mode.
- ✗ **D. Storage optimized I family:** it is built for very high local disk IOPS (for example NoSQL databases), not for maximum CPU throughput.

## Key idea
Sustained CPU-heavy work such as encoding belongs on compute optimized C family instances; burstable T instances are for low average CPU.

stem: An in-memory analytics application needs hundreds of GiB of RAM per instance. Which instance family fits?

choices.text: Burstable general-purpose instances such as T family
Compute optimized instances such as the C family
Accelerated computing instances with GPUs only
Memory optimized instances such as R or X families

explanation:
## Matching memory needs to instance families
Each instance family has a typical ratio of memory to vCPU:
- **Compute optimized, C family**: about 2 GiB per vCPU.
- **General purpose, M family**: about 4 GiB per vCPU.
- **Memory optimized, R family**: about 8 GiB per vCPU, for example `r7i.8xlarge` with 256 GiB.
- **Memory optimized, X family**: about 16 GiB per vCPU or more, with sizes reaching several TiB; **High Memory U family** instances go even higher.
## Why in-memory analytics needs them
In-memory analytics engines (for example SAP HANA, Spark caching or large in-memory databases) keep the working data set in RAM. If the data does not fit, the application spills to disk or fails, so the deciding factor is RAM per instance, not CPU.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Burstable T family:** the largest T sizes offer tens of GiB of RAM, not hundreds, and their credit-based CPU is meant for light, intermittent workloads.
- ✗ **B. Compute optimized C family:** the memory-to-vCPU ratio is low, so reaching hundreds of GiB means paying for far more CPU than needed.
- ✗ **C. GPU accelerated computing:** GPUs speed up parallel math such as machine learning or rendering; buying them only for RAM wastes money and does not target the requirement.
- ✓ **D. Memory optimized R or X families (correct):** they offer a high memory-to-vCPU ratio and sizes with hundreds of GiB up to TiBs of RAM, which is what in-memory analytics needs.

## Key idea
When the requirement is RAM per instance (in-memory workloads), choose memory optimized R or X instances, not compute, burstable or GPU instances.

stem: An application runs short, event-driven tasks for a few seconds each, triggered by S3 uploads. Which compute option fits best?

choices.text: Amazon EMR
AWS Lambda
Amazon EC2
AWS Batch

explanation:
## AWS Lambda for short, event-driven tasks
AWS Lambda runs your code in response to events without servers to manage. You upload a function, connect it to an event source, and Lambda runs one execution per event.
- **Event sources**: S3 uploads, SQS messages, API Gateway requests, EventBridge rules and more.
- **Scaling**: many uploads at once lead to many concurrent executions automatically.
- **Pricing**: you pay per request and per millisecond of run time, so tasks that last a few seconds cost very little and idle time costs nothing.
- **Limit**: a single invocation can run up to 15 minutes, which is ample for seconds-long tasks.
Example: an upload to `s3://uploads/` triggers a function that validates the file and writes metadata to DynamoDB in two seconds.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon EMR:** it runs big data clusters (Spark, Hadoop) for large-scale processing; starting or keeping a cluster for seconds-long per-file tasks is slow and costly.
- ✓ **B. AWS Lambda (correct):** it is triggered directly by S3 events, runs each short task on demand, scales automatically and charges only for the seconds of execution.
- ✗ **C. Amazon EC2:** instances must be provisioned, patched and kept running (and paid for) even when no uploads arrive, and extra code is needed to receive the events.
- ✗ **D. AWS Batch:** it queues and schedules batch jobs on managed compute, which adds job scheduling and container startup overhead that does not suit seconds-long tasks per upload.

## Key idea
Short, per-event tasks triggered by S3 fit Lambda; EMR, Batch and EC2 are for larger or long-running workloads.

stem: A read-heavy application's RDS database is overloaded by read queries. Which change improves performance?

choices.text: Enable Multi-AZ and send reads to the standby instance
Increase the backup retention period of the database
Add RDS read replicas and route read queries to them
Enable storage auto scaling to add more disk space

explanation:
## Scaling reads on Amazon RDS
A single RDS primary instance handles both writes and reads. When read traffic dominates, the primary runs out of CPU or I/O even though writes are light.
## Read replicas
A **read replica** is a separate DB instance that receives changes from the primary through **asynchronous** replication and accepts read-only queries.
- MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL support up to 15 read replicas per source.
- Each replica has its own endpoint; the application sends `SELECT` traffic to replicas and writes to the primary.
- Replicas can be in the same AZ, another AZ or another Region.
Example: reporting queries and product page reads go to two replicas, cutting the primary's CPU from 90% to 40%.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Multi-AZ standby for reads:** in a Multi-AZ instance deployment the standby does not accept connections; it exists only for failover. (Only the separate Multi-AZ DB cluster option has readable standbys.)
- ✗ **B. Longer backup retention:** this only keeps automated backups for more days; it adds no capacity for queries.
- ✓ **C. Read replicas with read routing (correct):** reads move to separate instances, which takes load off the primary and adds read capacity.
- ✗ **D. Storage auto scaling:** it adds disk space when free storage runs low; the problem is read load on CPU and I/O, not full disks.

## Key idea
Read-heavy RDS load is solved with read replicas; a Multi-AZ instance standby is for availability and cannot serve reads.

stem: A session store needs sub-millisecond latency and must handle millions of reads per second. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon ElastiCache
Amazon RDS MySQL
Amazon Redshift
Amazon S3 Standard

explanation:
## Why session stores use an in-memory cache
Session data (login state, shopping cart) is small, read on almost every request, and must be fast. Disk-based databases add milliseconds per lookup; an in-memory store answers in well under a millisecond.
## Amazon ElastiCache
ElastiCache is a managed in-memory data store with Valkey, Redis OSS or Memcached engines.
- Data lives in RAM, giving sub-millisecond latency.
- Cluster mode spreads keys across shards, and read replicas add read capacity, so a cluster can handle millions of operations per second.
- Keys can expire automatically with a TTL, for example `SET session:abc123 ... EX 1800` for a 30-minute session.
- Multi-AZ with automatic failover (Valkey and Redis OSS) keeps sessions available.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Amazon ElastiCache (correct):** it keeps sessions in memory with sub-millisecond latency and scales to millions of reads per second through sharding and replicas.
- ✗ **B. Amazon RDS MySQL:** it is a disk-based relational database with typical millisecond latencies, and one primary with a few replicas struggles to serve millions of reads per second.
- ✗ **C. Amazon Redshift:** it is a data warehouse for analytical queries over large data sets; queries take far longer than a millisecond and it is not built for high-rate key lookups.
- ✗ **D. Amazon S3 Standard:** it is object storage accessed over HTTP with latency in the tens of milliseconds, far too slow for per-request session lookups.

## Key idea
Sub-millisecond latency at millions of reads per second means an in-memory store such as ElastiCache, not a disk-based database, warehouse or object store.

stem: A serverless application's Lambda functions open many connections to an RDS database and exhaust connection limits. Which service helps?

choices.text: Amazon SQS FIFO
Amazon Route 53
Amazon CloudFront
Amazon RDS Proxy

explanation:
## Why Lambda exhausts database connections
Every Lambda execution environment runs its own copy of your code, so each one opens its own database connection. When traffic bursts, Lambda can start hundreds of environments in seconds, and a relational database such as RDS for MySQL has a fixed `max_connections` limit based on instance memory and settings. Once the limit is reached, new connections are refused and the application fails.
## How RDS Proxy helps
Amazon RDS Proxy is a fully managed database proxy that sits between the application and an RDS or Aurora database.
- It keeps a **pool** of connections open to the database and lets many client connections share them (multiplexing).
- Lambda functions connect to the proxy endpoint instead of the database endpoint; the proxy absorbs the burst.
- It can read database credentials from AWS Secrets Manager and supports IAM authentication.
- During a Multi-AZ failover it keeps client connections open and redirects them, which shortens the outage seen by the app.
Example: 500 concurrent Lambda environments connect to the proxy, which serves them over a much smaller set of database connections.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon SQS FIFO:** a queue can buffer work so fewer functions run at once, but it is not a connection manager, and FIFO ordering adds throughput limits without pooling any connections to the database.
- ✗ **B. Amazon Route 53:** it is a DNS service that resolves names to endpoints; it has no visibility into database sessions and cannot share or limit connections.
- ✗ **C. Amazon CloudFront:** a CDN caches HTTP responses at edge locations; Lambda-to-database connections are made from inside AWS and never pass through CloudFront.
- ✓ **D. Amazon RDS Proxy (correct):** it pools and reuses database connections, so bursts of Lambda invocations no longer open one database connection each and the connection limit is not exhausted.

## Key idea
When many short-lived Lambda functions overwhelm a relational database's connection limit, put RDS Proxy in front of it to pool connections, rather than a queue, DNS or a CDN.

stem: A gaming application needs a database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale and flexible schemas. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Redshift
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon RDS for MySQL
Amazon Athena

explanation:
## Amazon DynamoDB in one paragraph
DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL database for key-value and document data. Each item is found by its **partition key** (optionally plus a sort key), and DynamoDB spreads partitions across many servers, so reads and writes by key stay in the single-digit millisecond range whether the table holds a few items or many terabytes.
## Why it suits games
- **Flexible schema**: only the key attributes are fixed; one player item can have `inventory` and another can have `guild` without a schema migration.
- **Scale**: on-demand capacity mode absorbs sudden player spikes without capacity planning; provisioned mode suits steady traffic.
- **Extras**: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) adds microsecond cached reads, and global tables replicate data to several Regions for players worldwide.
Example: a global secondary index with `GameId` as the partition key and `Score` as the sort key returns a game's top players with one query.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon Redshift:** it is a columnar data warehouse built for complex analytical queries over large datasets, not for millisecond lookups of individual player records, and it uses fixed table schemas.
- ✓ **B. Amazon DynamoDB (correct):** it delivers consistent single-digit millisecond latency at virtually any scale and stores schemaless items, which matches the gaming requirements.
- ✗ **C. Amazon RDS for MySQL:** it is a relational database with a fixed schema that mainly scales up by resizing one writer instance, so it cannot promise consistent latency at any scale the way DynamoDB can.
- ✗ **D. Amazon Athena:** it runs ad hoc SQL over files in S3; queries take seconds and it is not an operational database that an application writes game state to.

## Key idea
For key-based access with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale and a flexible schema, choose DynamoDB; relational and analytics services fit other patterns.

stem: A company serves static and dynamic content to global users and wants lower latency. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
AWS Direct Connect
Amazon VPC peering
Amazon CloudFront

explanation:
## What a content delivery network does
Amazon CloudFront is AWS's content delivery network (CDN). It runs hundreds of edge locations around the world; users are routed to a nearby edge instead of travelling all the way to your origin (an S3 bucket, a load balancer, EC2 or any HTTP server).
## Static and dynamic content
- **Static content** such as images, CSS and videos is cached at the edge, so repeat requests are answered without reaching the origin.
- **Dynamic content** such as personalised API responses cannot be cached, but CloudFront still speeds it up: TLS is terminated close to the user, connections to the origin are kept open and reused, and traffic between edge and origin rides the AWS global network.
- Cache behaviors let you set different caching rules per path, for example cache `/static/*` for a day and forward `/api/*` without caching.
Example: a user in Sydney loading a site hosted in `us-east-1` gets images from a Sydney edge and API calls over an already open, optimised connection.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AWS Site-to-Site VPN:** it creates encrypted IPsec tunnels between an on-premises network and a VPC; public end users on the internet do not use it and it adds no caching or edge presence.
- ✗ **B. AWS Direct Connect:** it is a dedicated private link from a data centre to AWS, useful for corporate network traffic, but it does nothing for anonymous users browsing from around the world.
- ✗ **C. Amazon VPC peering:** it privately connects two VPCs so their resources can talk; it is internal networking and does not bring content closer to end users.
- ✓ **D. Amazon CloudFront (correct):** it caches static content at edge locations near users and accelerates dynamic requests over optimised connections to the origin, cutting latency for a global audience.

## Key idea
To lower latency for global users of both static and dynamic content, use CloudFront edge locations; VPN, Direct Connect and peering only connect private networks.

stem: A multiplayer game uses UDP and needs static IP addresses with fast routing to the nearest healthy Region. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Global Accelerator
Application Load Balancer
Amazon Route 53 simple
Amazon CloudFront

explanation:
## How AWS Global Accelerator works
Global Accelerator gives an application two **static anycast IP addresses** that are announced from AWS edge locations worldwide. A player's packets enter the AWS network at the nearest edge and then travel over the AWS backbone to an endpoint group in a Region.
- It supports both **TCP and UDP** listeners, so real-time game traffic works.
- Endpoints can be Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers, EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses in several Regions.
- It continuously health-checks endpoints and shifts traffic away from an unhealthy Region without any DNS change, because the IPs never change.
## Why static IPs matter
Game clients, firewalls and partners can allow-list two fixed IPs once. Failover happens behind those IPs, so clients are not affected by DNS caching.
Example: players in Europe enter at a Frankfurt edge and reach `eu-central-1`; if that Region fails, the same IPs now lead to `eu-west-1`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. AWS Global Accelerator (correct):** it provides static anycast IPs, supports UDP, and routes each user over the AWS network to the closest healthy regional endpoint with fast health-based failover.
- ✗ **B. Application Load Balancer:** it handles only HTTP, HTTPS and gRPC at layer 7, does not support UDP, has no static IP addresses and lives in a single Region.
- ✗ **C. Amazon Route 53 simple:** simple routing returns the same record set without health checks, and any DNS-based failover is still delayed by client DNS caching and does not provide static IPs.
- ✗ **D. Amazon CloudFront:** it serves HTTP and HTTPS (including WebSocket) content; it does not proxy arbitrary UDP game traffic.

## Key idea
Non-HTTP (UDP) traffic that needs static IPs and fast failover to the nearest healthy Region points to Global Accelerator, not CloudFront or DNS routing.

stem: An application needs a load balancer that handles millions of TCP connections per second with ultra-low latency and static IPs per AZ. Which option fits?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
Classic Load Balancer

explanation:
## The Elastic Load Balancing family
- **Application Load Balancer (ALB)**: layer 7, understands HTTP, routes by path, host or header.
- **Network Load Balancer (NLB)**: layer 4, forwards TCP, UDP and TLS connections without reading the payload.
- **Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB)**: layer 3, sends packets through fleets of security appliances.
- **Classic Load Balancer (CLB)**: the previous generation, kept only for existing legacy workloads.
## What makes NLB different
Because NLB does not inspect application content, it can handle millions of requests per second with very low latency and scale for sudden spikes. It gives the load balancer **one static IP address per Availability Zone**, and you can assign your own Elastic IP to each AZ. It can also preserve the client source IP.
Example: a trading gateway whose partners allow-list IPs gets an NLB with an Elastic IP in each of three AZs, and partners only ever see those three addresses.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Application Load Balancer:** it processes HTTP at layer 7, which adds latency, and its IP addresses change as it scales, so it cannot offer a static IP per AZ.
- ✗ **B. Gateway Load Balancer:** it is designed to insert third-party firewalls and inspection appliances using GENEVE encapsulation, not to front an application's TCP clients.
- ✓ **C. Network Load Balancer (correct):** it works at layer 4 for TCP, is built for millions of connections per second at ultra-low latency, and provides a static (or Elastic) IP address in each AZ.
- ✗ **D. Classic Load Balancer:** it is a legacy load balancer with lower performance and no static IP addresses; AWS recommends migrating off it.

## Key idea
Extreme TCP performance plus fixed per-AZ IP addresses means NLB; ALB is for HTTP-aware routing and GWLB is for appliances.

stem: An application needs to route requests to different microservices based on URL paths such as /api and /images. Which load balancer fits?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer with path-based rules
Gateway Load Balancer with GENEVE tunnels
Route 53 weighted records for each service
Network Load Balancer with TCP listeners

explanation:
## Layer 7 routing with ALB listener rules
An Application Load Balancer reads each HTTP request, so its listener rules can make decisions based on the content of the request:
- **path-pattern**, such as `/api/*` or `/images/*`
- **host-header**, such as `shop.example.com`
- HTTP headers, HTTP method, query strings and source IP
Each rule forwards matching requests to a **target group**, which can hold EC2 instances, IP addresses (for example ECS tasks) or Lambda functions. Rules are evaluated in priority order, with a default action for anything that does not match.
Example: one ALB with a rule `/api/*` forwarding to the API service's target group and `/images/*` forwarding to the image service, all behind a single DNS name.
This is a common way to put several microservices behind one entry point.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Application Load Balancer with path-based rules (correct):** it inspects the URL path of every HTTP request and forwards `/api` and `/images` to different target groups, which is exactly what is needed.
- ✗ **B. Gateway Load Balancer with GENEVE tunnels:** it passes packets transparently through inspection appliances at layer 3 and never looks at HTTP paths.
- ✗ **C. Route 53 weighted records for each service:** DNS only sees the hostname being resolved, never the URL path, and weights split traffic by percentage rather than by request content.
- ✗ **D. Network Load Balancer with TCP listeners:** it forwards connections at layer 4 without parsing HTTP, so it cannot route by path.

## Key idea
Any routing decision that depends on the URL path, host or header requires a layer 7 load balancer, which on AWS is the ALB.

stem: A company must ingest real-time clickstream data from thousands of sources and process it within seconds. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
AWS Snowball Edge devices
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive

explanation:
## Streaming data versus stored data
Clickstream events arrive continuously from many producers and are most valuable within seconds. A streaming service stores them as an ordered, replayable log that several consumers can read in real time.
## How Kinesis Data Streams works
- A stream is split into **shards**; each shard accepts up to 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s of writes, and on-demand mode adds shards automatically.
- Producers (web servers, SDKs, the Kinesis Producer Library) put records with a partition key that decides the shard, keeping order per key.
- Consumers such as AWS Lambda, applications using the Kinesis Client Library, or Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink read records within about a second of arrival.
- Data is retained for 24 hours by default and can be kept up to 365 days, so consumers can replay it.
Example: thousands of browsers send page-view events; a Lambda consumer updates a real-time dashboard while a second consumer detects fraud.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL:** it is a transactional database; thousands of sources inserting rows continuously would strain it, and it offers no streaming consumers or replayable ordered log.
- ✗ **B. AWS Snowball Edge devices:** they are physical devices shipped to move data offline in bulk, a process that takes days, not seconds.
- ✓ **C. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams (correct):** it ingests high-volume events from thousands of producers and makes them available to consumers within seconds, which is real-time stream processing.
- ✗ **D. Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive:** it is the lowest-cost archive storage class with retrieval measured in hours, the opposite of real-time processing.

## Key idea
Real-time ingestion from many producers with processing in seconds means a streaming service such as Kinesis Data Streams, not a database, an offline transfer device or an archive.

stem: Streaming data must be delivered to S3 in batches, converted to Parquet, with no code to manage. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SQS standard
Amazon SNS topics
AWS Step Functions
Amazon Data Firehose

explanation:
## What Amazon Data Firehose does
Amazon Data Firehose (formerly Kinesis Data Firehose) is a fully managed delivery service: producers send records and Firehose writes them to a destination such as Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Splunk or an HTTP endpoint. There are no servers or consumer code to run.
## Features that match this question
- **Buffering**: records are grouped by size or time interval (for example every 128 MB or 300 seconds) and written as larger S3 objects.
- **Record format conversion**: JSON input can be converted to Apache Parquet or ORC using a schema from the AWS Glue Data Catalog, which makes later Athena queries faster and cheaper.
- **Optional transforms and partitioning**: a Lambda function can reshape records, and dynamic partitioning writes to prefixes such as `year=2026/month=09/`.
Example: application logs flow into a Firehose stream that buffers them, converts them to Parquet and writes them to an S3 data lake.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon SQS standard:** a queue only holds messages until a consumer polls them; you would have to write and run the consumer that batches, converts and writes to S3.
- ✗ **B. Amazon SNS topics:** SNS pushes each message to subscribers immediately; it has no batching into files and no Parquet conversion.
- ✗ **C. AWS Step Functions:** it orchestrates steps you define, so you would still need to build the batching and format conversion yourself, and it is not designed to ingest a continuous stream.
- ✓ **D. Amazon Data Firehose (correct):** it delivers streaming data to S3 in buffered batches and can convert records to Parquet natively, all as a managed service with no code to manage.

## Key idea
Managed "stream to S3, batched and converted to Parquet" is Data Firehose; queues, topics and workflows need custom code for the same result.

stem: Analysts want to run SQL queries directly on data in S3 without loading it into a database. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon ElastiCache
Amazon Athena
Amazon RDS
Amazon DynamoDB

explanation:
## Querying data where it lives
Amazon Athena is a serverless, interactive query service. You define tables over files already in Amazon S3 (usually in the AWS Glue Data Catalog), then run standard SQL; Athena reads the files directly, with no loading step and no cluster to manage.
- Works with CSV, JSON, Apache Parquet, ORC and other formats.
- You pay based on the amount of data each query scans, so columnar formats, compression and partitioning (for example by `dt=2026-09-29`) cut both cost and query time.
- Results are written back to an S3 location you choose.
Example: `SELECT status, count(*) FROM access_logs WHERE dt = '2026-09-29' GROUP BY status;` runs directly on ALB log files stored in S3.
This makes Athena a common choice for ad hoc analysis of logs and data lakes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon ElastiCache:** it is an in-memory cache (Valkey, Redis OSS or Memcached) for fast key lookups; it cannot query files stored in S3 with SQL.
- ✓ **B. Amazon Athena (correct):** it runs serverless SQL directly against data in S3 without loading it into a database first, exactly what the analysts want.
- ✗ **C. Amazon RDS:** it is a managed relational database, so the data would first have to be imported into database tables, which the requirement rules out.
- ✗ **D. Amazon DynamoDB:** it is a NoSQL key-value database; data would have to be imported into tables, and it is not a SQL engine for S3 files.

## Key idea
SQL directly on S3 files with no loading and no servers means Athena; databases and caches require the data to be loaded first.

stem: Which TWO options reduce latency for a globally distributed read-heavy application backed by Aurora MySQL? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Aurora Global Database with read replicas in other Regions
Moving the database to a single Availability Zone
Disabling query caching on the application layer
A larger writer instance in a single Region only
CloudFront caching for cacheable API responses

explanation:
## Two ways to bring reads closer to users
Latency for a global audience mostly comes from distance: a request from Asia to a database in `us-east-1` crosses an ocean each time.
## Aurora Global Database
Aurora Global Database has one primary Region that accepts writes and secondary Regions with read-only clusters. Replication happens at the storage layer with typical lag under a second, so users in each Region can read from a local copy, and a secondary Region can be promoted for disaster recovery.
## Caching at the edge
Many API responses, such as a product catalogue or configuration, are identical for many users. CloudFront can cache them at edge locations for a chosen TTL, so repeat requests never reach the application or database at all.
- Only cache what is safe to share; forward personalised requests to the origin.
Example: a read-heavy store serves catalogue calls from CloudFront and other reads from the nearest Aurora secondary Region.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Aurora Global Database with read replicas in other Regions (correct):** each Region gets a local read-only copy of the data with low replication lag, so reads no longer travel to a distant primary.
- ✗ **B. Moving the database to a single Availability Zone:** this removes the standby and lowers availability, and it does nothing about the distance between global users and the database.
- ✗ **C. Disabling query caching on the application layer:** turning caching off sends every request to the database, raising latency and load rather than lowering it.
- ✗ **D. A larger writer instance in a single Region only:** more CPU and memory do not shorten the distance to users in other continents, and read-heavy traffic still crosses the globe.
- ✓ **E. CloudFront caching for cacheable API responses (correct):** repeat requests are answered from an edge location near the user, removing both the network distance and the database round trip.

## Key idea
For global read-heavy traffic, move data closer to users with cross-Region read copies and edge caching, not with bigger instances in one place.

stem: A company runs a fleet of Linux EC2 instances that must all read and write the same files concurrently. Which TWO services provide this shared file storage? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Amazon EC2 instance store volumes
Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway
Amazon FSx for Lustre
Amazon EFS

explanation:
## Block, object and file storage
- **Block storage** (EBS, instance store) appears as a disk attached to one instance.
- **Object storage** (S3) is accessed through an API, not mounted as a normal file system.
- **File storage** offers a shared directory tree that many machines can mount at once, with file locking and POSIX permissions.
## Shared file systems for Linux on AWS
- **Amazon EFS** is a serverless NFS file system that grows and shrinks automatically. Thousands of EC2 instances, containers and Lambda functions across multiple AZs can mount it concurrently.
- **Amazon FSx for Lustre** is a high-performance parallel file system for Linux workloads such as HPC, machine learning and media rendering. Many clients mount it at once, and it can be linked to an S3 bucket.
Example: a render farm mounts FSx for Lustre at `/scratch`, while a web fleet mounts EFS at `/shared/uploads`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon EC2 instance store volumes:** they are temporary disks physically attached to one host; other instances cannot mount them and data is lost when the instance stops.
- ✗ **B. Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval:** it is an archive storage class with retrieval times of minutes to hours, and it is object storage rather than a mountable file system.
- ✗ **C. AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway:** it presents virtual tapes to on-premises backup software and stores them in S3 and Glacier; it is not a live shared file system.
- ✓ **D. Amazon FSx for Lustre (correct):** it is a shared POSIX file system that many Linux instances mount at the same time for concurrent, high-throughput reads and writes.
- ✓ **E. Amazon EFS (correct):** it is a fully managed NFS file system that many Linux instances across AZs can mount and use concurrently.

## Key idea
When many Linux instances must read and write the same files at once, use a shared file system (EFS or FSx for Lustre), not block volumes, archives or virtual tapes.

stem: Log files in S3 are accessed often for 30 days, rarely for a year, and then must be kept for seven years for compliance. Which approach minimizes cost?

choices.text: Store the logs on large EBS volumes attached to a dedicated logging instance
Move objects to Glacier Deep Archive on the first day
Lifecycle rules moving objects to Standard-IA, then Glacier Deep Archive
Keep all objects in S3 Standard for the entire seven years

explanation:
## S3 storage classes follow access frequency
Each S3 storage class trades storage price against retrieval cost and speed:
- **S3 Standard**: higher storage price, no retrieval fee; best for data read often.
- **S3 Standard-IA**: cheaper storage, per-GB retrieval fee, 30-day minimum storage duration; best for data read rarely but needed in milliseconds.
- **S3 Glacier Deep Archive**: the lowest storage price, 180-day minimum, retrieval within hours; best for compliance copies.
## Lifecycle rules automate the moves
A lifecycle configuration tells S3 to transition objects between classes and expire them by age.
Example rule for this log bucket:
- day 0 to 30: stay in S3 Standard while logs are read often
- day 30: transition to Standard-IA for the year of rare access
- day 365: transition to Glacier Deep Archive for long-term retention
- after seven years: expire (delete) the objects
Each object always sits in the cheapest class that still meets how it is being used.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A.:** Store the logs on large EBS volumes attached to a dedicated logging instance: EBS is priced per provisioned GB, far above archive tiers, and you also pay for the instance; seven years of logs would be very expensive.
- ✗ **B. Move objects to Glacier Deep Archive on the first day:** logs read frequently in the first 30 days would need restores that take hours and incur retrieval charges, breaking the access pattern.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Lifecycle rules moving objects to Standard-IA, then Glacier Deep Archive: they match each phase of the logs' life to the cheapest suitable class automatically, so cost drops as access declines.
- ✗ **D. Keep all objects in S3 Standard for the entire seven years:** Standard is the most expensive class to keep rarely read data in, so years of retention at that rate waste money.

## Key idea
Data whose access drops over time should move through storage classes via lifecycle rules, not sit in one class for its whole life.

stem: A dataset has unpredictable access patterns, and the team does not want to manage lifecycle rules. Which storage class fits?

choices.text: S3 Standard-IA storage
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Glacier Instant tier
S3 One Zone-IA storage

explanation:
## How S3 Intelligent-Tiering works
S3 Intelligent-Tiering watches each object's access and moves it between tiers automatically:
- **Frequent Access** tier by default.
- **Infrequent Access** tier after 30 consecutive days without access.
- **Archive Instant Access** tier after 90 days without access.
- Optional **Archive Access** and **Deep Archive Access** tiers you can enable for data that can wait for asynchronous retrieval.
When an object in the Infrequent or Archive Instant tier is accessed, it moves back to Frequent Access automatically.
## The cost model
There are no retrieval fees for the automatic tiers, only a small monthly monitoring charge per object. Objects smaller than 128 KB are not monitored and are always billed at the Frequent Access rate.
Example: a data lake where some datasets are hot for a week and others are untouched for months saves money without anyone writing lifecycle rules.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. S3 Standard-IA storage:** it charges a per-GB retrieval fee, so if the unpredictable data turns out to be read often, costs can exceed S3 Standard, and nothing moves objects for you.
- ✓ **B. S3 Intelligent-Tiering (correct):** it moves objects between access tiers automatically based on actual use, with no retrieval fees and no lifecycle rules to maintain, ideal for unpredictable access.
- ✗ **C. S3 Glacier Instant tier:** Glacier Instant Retrieval is priced for data read about once a quarter, with higher retrieval fees and a 90-day minimum, which is costly if access spikes.
- ✗ **D. S3 One Zone-IA storage:** it keeps data in a single AZ, charges retrieval fees and does not adapt to changing access, so it neither solves the unpredictability nor keeps multi-AZ resilience.

## Key idea
When access patterns are unknown or changing, let S3 Intelligent-Tiering pick the tier; fixed infrequent-access classes penalise surprise reads.

stem: Easily reproducible thumbnail images are accessed infrequently. The company wants the lowest-cost S3 option with millisecond access. Which fits?

choices.text: S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Express One Zone
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Standard

explanation:
## Resilience versus price in S3
Most S3 storage classes store data across at least three Availability Zones. **S3 One Zone-IA** stores data in a single AZ, which makes its storage cheaper than Standard-IA (roughly 20% less), but the data is lost if that AZ is destroyed.
- Like Standard-IA, it returns data in milliseconds, charges a per-GB retrieval fee and has a 30-day minimum storage duration.
- It fits data you can recreate, such as thumbnails, transcoded copies or secondary backups.
## Do not confuse it with S3 Express One Zone
S3 Express One Zone also lives in one AZ, but it is a high-performance class in directory buckets that delivers single-digit millisecond latency for frequently accessed data, with a higher storage price than S3 Standard.
Example: original photos stay in S3 Standard; their thumbnails, which can be regenerated from the originals, go to One Zone-IA.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. S3 One Zone-IA (correct):** among the options it is the cheapest class that still returns objects in milliseconds, and its single-AZ risk is acceptable because the thumbnails can be regenerated.
- ✗ **B. S3 Express One Zone:** it is optimised for the fastest, most frequent access and has a higher storage price than S3 Standard, the opposite of low-cost storage for rarely read data.
- ✗ **C. S3 Glacier Deep Archive:** storage is cheaper, but restores take hours, so it fails the millisecond access requirement.
- ✗ **D. S3 Standard:** it offers millisecond access but costs clearly more per GB than One Zone-IA for data that is rarely read.

## Key idea
Reproducible, infrequently accessed data that still needs instant access belongs in One Zone-IA; Express One Zone is about speed, not savings.

stem: A company runs a steady workload on EC2 24/7 for the next three years, but may change instance families. Which purchase option fits?

choices.text: On-Demand Instances only
Compute Savings Plans
Dedicated Hosts only
Spot Instances only

explanation:
## Commitment-based discounts for EC2
AWS offers lower prices when you commit to steady usage for one or three years:
- **Savings Plans** commit to a dollar amount of compute per hour (for example `$10/hour`) and discount usage up to that amount.
- **Compute Savings Plans** apply automatically to EC2 in any instance family, size, Region, operating system or tenancy, and also to AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda.
- **EC2 Instance Savings Plans** give a larger discount but are tied to one instance family in one Region.
- **Reserved Instances** are the older model, tied to specific instance attributes.
## Why flexibility matters here
The workload is steady for three years, which makes a commitment worthwhile, but the team might move from `m5` to `m7g` or change sizes. A Compute Savings Plan keeps applying the discount after such a change.
Example: a three-year Compute Savings Plan covers a fleet moved from Intel `c5` instances to Graviton `c7g` without losing the discount.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. On-Demand Instances only:** they have no commitment, but a workload running 24/7 for three years pays full price the whole time, missing large available discounts.
- ✓ **B. Compute Savings Plans (correct):** they give a significant discount for committed steady usage over three years while still applying if the company changes instance family, size or Region.
- ✗ **C. Dedicated Hosts only:** they reserve a whole physical server, mainly for licensing or compliance needs, and cost more than shared-tenancy instances; they add no pricing flexibility.
- ✗ **D. Spot Instances only:** they are cheap but AWS can reclaim them with a two-minute warning, which is unsuitable for a steady workload that must run continuously.

## Key idea
Steady usage plus the need to change instance families points to Compute Savings Plans, which trade some discount for flexibility.

stem: A fault-tolerant batch job can be interrupted and restarted. Which EC2 option minimizes cost?

choices.text: Dedicated Instances
Reserved Instances
On-Demand Instances
Spot Instances

explanation:
## How Spot Instances work
Spot Instances use spare EC2 capacity at discounts of up to 90% compared with On-Demand prices. The trade-off is that AWS can reclaim the capacity when it needs it, giving a **two-minute interruption notice** (plus an earlier rebalance recommendation in many cases).
## Designing for interruption
- Save progress with checkpoints, for example to S3, so a restarted job resumes instead of starting over.
- Use many instance types and AZs (for example with an Auto Scaling group or EC2 Fleet using a capacity-optimised allocation strategy) to reduce interruptions.
- Services like AWS Batch and EMR can run on Spot and retry interrupted work automatically.
Example: an image-processing batch job splits work into small chunks in an SQS queue; if an instance is reclaimed, its unfinished chunk returns to the queue and another instance picks it up.
Workloads that are fault-tolerant and flexible on timing are the classic Spot use case.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Dedicated Instances:** they run on hardware dedicated to one customer and cost more than regular instances; they address isolation needs, not cost.
- ✗ **B. Reserved Instances:** they need a one- or three-year commitment for steady usage, which does not fit an occasional batch job and saves less than Spot.
- ✗ **C. On-Demand Instances:** they are never interrupted, but you pay the full price for a reliability the fault-tolerant job does not need.
- ✓ **D. Spot Instances (correct):** they give the deepest EC2 discount, and the job's ability to be interrupted and restarted removes the main drawback of Spot.

## Key idea
When work tolerates interruption, Spot is the cheapest EC2 option; reservations are for steady workloads and On-Demand for work that must not be interrupted.

stem: A web application's Auto Scaling group runs at 10% CPU most of the time on large instances. Which change reduces cost most?

choices.text: Add more large instances to spread the load more evenly
Purchase Reserved Instances for the current large instance size
Right-size to smaller instances and keep target tracking scaling
Disable Auto Scaling and keep a fixed fleet of large instances

explanation:
## What right-sizing means
Right-sizing is matching instance type and size to the real resource needs of a workload. An instance that averages 10% CPU is mostly paid-for idle capacity.
- Tools such as AWS Compute Optimizer and Cost Explorer's rightsizing recommendations analyse CloudWatch metrics and suggest smaller or different instance types.
- Check memory, network and disk metrics as well as CPU before downsizing.
## Right-size, then scale, then commit
- A **target tracking** scaling policy keeps a metric such as average CPU near a target (for example 50%) by adding or removing instances as demand changes.
- Smaller instances make scaling finer-grained, so capacity follows demand more closely.
- Only after sizing is correct should you buy Savings Plans or Reserved Instances, so the commitment is not locked to waste.
Example: an Auto Scaling group of `m5.2xlarge` at 10% CPU is moved to `m5.large` with a 50% CPU target; it runs more instances at peak and fewer overnight, at a fraction of the cost.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Add more large instances to spread the load more evenly:** the fleet is already underused, so adding instances only increases cost and pushes utilisation even lower.
- ✗ **B.:** Purchase Reserved Instances for the current large instance size: the discount applies to capacity that is mostly idle, locking in waste for one or three years.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Right-size to smaller instances and keep target tracking scaling: it removes the paid-for idle capacity while scaling still adds instances when demand rises, which gives the biggest saving.
- ✗ **D.:** Disable Auto Scaling and keep a fixed fleet of large instances: a fixed fleet must be sized for peak and pays for it all the time, removing the savings that scaling provides.

## Key idea
Fix oversized instances first, then let scaling follow demand, and only then commit to discounts.

stem: An API receives only a few hundred requests per day with occasional spikes. Which compute option minimizes cost?

choices.text: A dedicated host for the API
An EKS cluster with three nodes
Two EC2 instances running 24/7
AWS Lambda behind API Gateway

explanation:
## Paying for idle versus paying per use
Server-based options (EC2, EKS nodes, dedicated hosts) bill for every hour they run, whether they serve one request or a million. For an API with a few hundred requests a day, almost all of those hours are idle.
## The serverless alternative
- **AWS Lambda** bills per request and per GB-second of execution time; when no requests arrive, the cost is zero. It scales out automatically for spikes.
- **Amazon API Gateway** also bills per API call received, with no hourly charge for REST or HTTP APIs.
- Lambda includes a monthly free tier of requests and compute time, and a few hundred requests per day costs very little.
Example: 300 requests a day that each run for 200 ms on a small Lambda function use a tiny fraction of the monthly free tier, while one small EC2 instance running all month is billed for every hour.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. A dedicated host for the API:** it reserves an entire physical server billed hourly, one of the most expensive ways to run a tiny workload.
- ✗ **B. An EKS cluster with three nodes:** you pay an hourly control plane fee plus three always-running worker nodes, a large fixed cost for a few hundred requests.
- ✗ **C. Two EC2 instances running 24/7:** they are billed every hour even though they sit idle most of the day, so the cost per request is very high.
- ✓ **D. AWS Lambda behind API Gateway (correct):** both are billed per request with nothing charged while idle, and they scale automatically for spikes, making this the cheapest option for low, bursty traffic.

## Key idea
For low and spiky traffic, pay-per-request serverless compute beats any option that bills for idle servers.

stem: A development database is used only during business hours. Which change reduces cost?

choices.text: Enable Multi-AZ for the development database
Stop the RDS instance outside business hours on a schedule
Purchase a three-year Reserved Instance for it
Increase the instance size so work finishes faster

explanation:
## Stopping an RDS instance
You can stop an Amazon RDS DB instance (or an Aurora cluster) when it is not needed. While it is stopped:
- you are **not billed for instance hours**, which is usually the largest part of the bill;
- you still pay for provisioned storage, backups and snapshots;
- data, configuration and endpoint are kept.
A stopped instance automatically starts again after **seven days**, so a schedule should stop it again as needed.
## Automating the schedule
Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to call the RDS `StopDBInstance` and `StartDBInstance` APIs at set times, or deploy the Instance Scheduler on AWS solution with tags.
Example: a development database running 10 hours a day on weekdays is stopped the rest of the time, roughly 70% of the week's hours, cutting its compute cost by a similar share.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Enable Multi-AZ for the development database:** it adds a standby instance, roughly doubling instance cost, to improve availability that a development database does not need.
- ✓ **B. Stop the RDS instance outside business hours on a schedule (correct):** instance-hour charges stop while it is not in use, so the company only pays compute for the hours developers actually work.
- ✗ **C. Purchase a three-year Reserved Instance for it:** a reservation is billed for every hour of the term, so the company would keep paying for nights and weekends when the database sits idle.
- ✗ **D. Increase the instance size so work finishes faster:** a larger instance costs more per hour, and development usage follows working hours, not job length, so it would still run all day.

## Key idea
For non-production databases used only part of the day, stop them on a schedule instead of paying for idle hours.

stem: A new application has unpredictable, intermittent database usage with long idle periods. Which option minimizes cost?

choices.text: Aurora Serverless v2
Self-managed MySQL on EC2
Provisioned Aurora cluster
RDS with Multi-AZ always on

explanation:
## Provisioned versus serverless database capacity
With a provisioned database you choose an instance size and pay for it every hour, even when there are no queries. For a new application with unknown and intermittent usage, that means paying for peak capacity during long idle periods.
## How Aurora Serverless v2 works
- Capacity is measured in **Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs)**; each ACU is about 2 GiB of memory with matching CPU and networking.
- You set a minimum and maximum ACU range, and Aurora scales in fine-grained steps within seconds as load changes.
- You pay for the ACUs actually used, billed per second, plus storage (and I/O when using the Aurora Standard configuration).
